name: Turkey Ants Climbing a Tree (Glass Noodles)
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Saucy noodles that absorb the braising liquid - reheats better than any stir-fried noodle. Verified source: full recipe, 2 servings, 479 cal / 16g protein, and the source already offers ground chicken as a swap. Confidence note: protein needs roughly doubling from the source ratio to clear our bar. | HARVEST: Source uses ground pork; adapt to turkey.
OVERRIDE Ground Pork: TITLE-PROTEIN SWAP + [BUMP x1.4]: source 160 g pork for 2; house 220 g ground turkey for the protein floor
intro_html: Ants climbing a tree gets its name from what it looks like in the bowl: little bits of meat clinging to slippery noodles. It is a Sichuan home cooking staple, built on doubanjiang, the fermented chili bean paste that makes so much of that province taste the way it does. The noodles soak up the braising liquid, which is exactly why this reheats better on day four than most noodle dishes do on day one. Each bowl runs 571 calories and 29 grams of protein for about $2.92.
ingredients_display: Doubanjiang (Lee Kum Kee (Chili Bean Sauce Toban Djan)): 4 oz (112 g)
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Chicken Broth, 3.6 cartons: ~$4.51. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 4 32oz cartons.
Pantry seasonings (salt, black pepper): ~$0.23. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $40.93 across 14 servings, so roughly $2.92 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $48.04 across 14 servings, roughly $3.43 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $19.68 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $67.72. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About $2.92 a bowl. The noodles and the chili bean paste are the two biggest lines, and the paste jar will still be working for you three recipes from now.
shop_smart: Doubanjiang is the most expensive thing in this batch, and it is also non-negotiable. Buy it at an Asian market where a large tub costs less than a small jar at the regular grocery store, then keep it in the fridge where it lasts a year.
The dried noodles are the single biggest line. Check the international aisle or an Asian market before the American brand shelf, because the same product often runs a third less two aisles over.

Chicken broth is a real line here because this dish braises in a lot of it. Buy the big carton or use bouillon dissolved in water, which costs a fraction and works fine in a sauce this heavily seasoned.
Ginger, garlic, and green onions are the aromatic base for pocket change. That is the cheapest flavor in Chinese cooking, and it is why home cooking beats takeout on both price and taste.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Soak the dried noodles in warm water until they are pliable but still firm, about 15 minutes, then drain them. They finish cooking in the braise, so undercook them now on purpose.
Heat the vegetable oil in a wok or wide pot, add the grated ginger and the white parts of the green onions, and cook 30 seconds.
Add the ground turkey and brown it into fine crumbles until it is cooked through to 165F.

Push the meat aside and fry the doubanjiang in the oil for 1 minute until it turns the fat a deep red. This step is what pulls the flavor out of the paste, and skipping it leaves the dish tasting flat and raw.
Add the chicken broth, soy sauce, and sugar, stir everything together, and bring it to a simmer.
Add the drained noodles, stir to submerge them, and simmer 6 to 8 minutes until they have drunk up most of the liquid and gone glossy. Stir often so they do not weld to the bottom.
Kill the heat, fold in the green onion tops, and move everything into your weighed pot.
portion_html: Set the full pot on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight you wrote down, and divide by 14. That is your per-container gram target. Use tongs and lift from the bottom each time so the meat that sinks gets shared out with the noodles that float. Each bowl lands at 571 calories and 29 grams of protein.

head.keywords: ants climbing a tree, sichuan noodles, doubanjiang, turkey meal prep, budget meal prep, chili bean sauce noodles
steps: Soak the dried noodles in warm water 15 minutes and drain.
Cook ginger and green onion whites in vegetable oil, then brown the ground turkey to 165F.
Fry the doubanjiang in the oil for 1 minute until it turns the fat red.
Add chicken broth, soy sauce, and sugar and bring to a simmer.
Add the noodles and simmer 6 to 8 minutes until the liquid is absorbed.
Fold in green onion tops and portion by weight into 14 containers.
